The Confederate Navy was the naval force of the Confederate States of America during the American Civil War from 1861 to 1865. Vastly outnumbered by the Union Navy, it could not achieve naval supremacy but pursued commerce raiding and technological innovation to break the Union blockade. The Confederacy inherited virtually no navy at secession; the South had to build one from scratch, seizing northern ships and constructing new vessels in limited facilities with minimal industrial capacity. Southern strategy centered on commerce raiding and blockade-running: privateers and warships like the CSS Alabama attacked Union merchant shipping to cripple northern trade, while blockade runners slipped through the Union cordon to bring supplies from Europe. The CSS Virginia, constructed by raising the sunken USS Merrimack and plating her with iron armor, was launched in 1862. She was revolutionary—the first warship sheathed entirely in iron, seemingly unsinkable. The Battle of Hampton Roads on March 9th, 1862, saw the CSS Virginia clash with the USS Monitor, the Union's new ironclad. Neither could sink the other, but the drawn battle proved that armored warships had replaced wooden vessels as the future of naval combat. Despite the Virginia's innovation, the Confederate Navy never overcame the Union's overwhelming numerical and industrial superiority. The blockade remained effective, strangling the Southern economy and preventing essential imports. The innovations the Confederate Navy developed—ironclads, semi-submersible vessels like the CSS Hunley, and naval mines—were adopted by navies worldwide. Confederate naval engineers thus influenced modern naval architecture despite their defeat.
